profile.reading:
Switch Las Vegas 7 sits at 7135 South Decatur Boulevard, Las Vegas, Nevada, in unincorporated Enterprise, Clark County. Data center industry aggregators place its opening year at 2008, and Switch's own February 2014 press release for the neighboring SUPERNAP 8 building describes Las Vegas 7 as "the original SUPERNAP," sitting several hundred yards away, corroborating that this building was the founding structure of what became Switch's sprawling Core Campus. Switch does not publish individual square footage, megawatt capacity, or redundancy-design figures for Las Vegas 7 on its current site; its historical role as the company's first purpose-built Las Vegas data center, from which the campus later expanded to include Las Vegas 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, and 14 among numbered buildings, is documented only indirectly through Switch's references to it in later press releases about newer buildings. Switch was founded by Rob Roy, who in 2002 acquired a former Enron-affiliated facility in Las Vegas at auction for 930,000 dollars, strategically sited over a fiber-optic backbone serving national technology companies; that 2002 acquisition is understood to be the origin of the Core Campus that Las Vegas 7 anchors. Switch's Core Campus is marketed today as offering up to 495 megawatts of power upon completion and 100 percent renewable energy, with Nevada's consumer-use-tax and property-tax abatement program, administered through the Governor's Office of Economic Development, cited by Switch as a business advantage of its home state.

Clark County's data center cluster, anchored substantially by Switch's Core Campus that Las Vegas 7 helped originate, has helped establish Las Vegas as a significant secondary U.S. data center market outside the major coastal and Northern Virginia hubs. Switch has since built a large solar and battery-storage generation program, including the Switch Station 1 and Switch Station 2 projects and the more recent Gigawatt Nevada development, to support its stated 100 percent renewable energy claim across its Nevada campuses, a program that traces its roots to the original site Las Vegas 7 anchors.

Wikipedia coverage states that in 2002 Roy acquired a former Enron facility in Las Vegas at auction for 930,000 dollars, strategically located over a fiber optic backbone serving technology companies nationwide, which became the foundation of the Las Vegas Core Campus. That campus has grown to eleven operating data centers spanning over 2 million square feet, with plans to reach 2.3 million square feet across 12 buildings. Switch also operates the Citadel Campus in Storey County in Northern Nevada, a separate 4 billion dollar, 1,000 plus acre development announced in January 2015, and a Grand Rapids, Michigan Pyramid Campus, but those are distinct from this Las Vegas registry cluster. In December 2022 DigitalBridge and IFM Investors completed an 11 billion dollar acquisition, taking Switch private. reading.body:
Switch Las Vegas 7 is the 2008 founding building of Switch's Las Vegas Core Campus, a sprawling multi-building complex in Clark County that the operator describes as offering up to 495 megawatts upon completion with 100 percent renewable energy. The operator does not publish individual capacity, square footage, or design specifications for Las Vegas 7 itself, only for the campus as a whole. Switch has built solar and battery storage generation including Switch Station 1, Switch Station 2, and Gigawatt Nevada to supply renewable power across its Nevada operations, a program that originated from this site.

Nevada has 26 mapped data center facilities, of which only two operators publish megawatt figures on their spec pages. The Core Campus that Las Vegas 7 anchors ranks third in the state by published capacity among facilities with disclosed figures, though the state's total published capacity across all facilities is 10.37 megawatts, a measurement that reflects sparse public disclosure rather than the actual buildout. Clark County's data center cluster, substantially anchored by Switch's Core Campus, has established Las Vegas as a significant secondary U.S. data center market outside the major coastal and Northern Virginia hubs.

The operator cites Nevada's property-tax and consumer-use-tax abatement programs administered through the Governor's Office of Economic Development as a business advantage. Switch does not publish street addresses on its official locations page, directing visitors instead to a contact form; the address given here comes from data center industry aggregator directories, not operator confirmation.
